summary: Defines two optional extensions to TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol. One lets the client and server agree on how long to wait before retransmitting, and the other lets the receiving side learn the total size of a file before the transfer begins. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2349.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers passing a file back and forth can agree how long to wait for an answer, and the receiver can ask how big the package is before it starts unpacking.

questions: what are the tftp timeout and tsize options
how does tftp negotiate transfer size
subtitle: Negotiate timeout and pre-transfer file size in TFTP.

tldr.problem: TFTP has a fixed timeout for retransmission and no way for the receiver to know the total file size before transfer begins, making it harder to allocate storage or choose optimal timeouts for different networks.
tldr.mechanism: The timeout option lets client and server agree on how many seconds to wait before retransmitting a lost packet (1 to 255 seconds). The transfer size (tsize) option lets the receiver learn the file size before transfer: in Read requests, the server responds with the size; in Write requests, the client provides it.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can tailor timeout values to network conditions and pre-allocate storage based on file size. This extension was later standardized more formally in RFC 2349.

facts.label: Tsize in Read
facts.value: Client sends 0, server responds with actual size

facts.label: Tsize in Write
facts.value: Client sends size, server echoes it

today: RFC 1784 defined these TFTP options as a standards-track proposal. It was later replaced and formalized in RFC 2349.

sections.title: TFTP Extensions for Flexibility
sections.content:
TFTP is simple and efficient for booting diskless machines, but it has limitations. The protocol uses a fixed retransmission timeout that may not suit all networks: satellite links need longer timeouts than LANs, and there is no standard way to determine file size before transfer begins. This RFC defines two options to address these issues.

Both options use the TFTP Option Extension mechanism, which allows client and server to negotiate optional parameters in the initial Read or Write Request and Option Acknowledgment (OACK) packets.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP is simple, but sometimes you need more flexibility. Two new options let you pick the timeout and learn the file size upfront.

sections.title: Timeout and Transfer Size Options
sections.content:
The timeout option ("timeout") specifies the number of seconds to wait before retransmitting (valid values 1 to 255). Both client and server must agree on the same timeout; the server's OACK must echo the client's proposed value. For example, a client might request a 1-second timeout on a fast LAN or 30 seconds for a slow wide-area link.

The tsize option ("tsize") negotiates file size. In Read Requests, the client sends tsize "0" and the server responds with the actual file size in bytes. In Write Requests, the client provides the file size, and the server echoes it back. If either side finds the size unacceptable (too large to store), they can abort with an ERROR packet (error code 3).
sections.plainLanguage: The timeout option is a number: how many seconds to wait for an answer before trying again. The tsize option lets you ask how big the file is before you start receiving it.

sections.title: Transfer Control and Error Handling
sections.content:
Once the client and server agree on these options via OACK, the transfer proceeds using the negotiated timeout and the receiver knows the total size upfront. For tsize in Write requests, the client supplies the size and the server echoes it; if the server cannot accommodate the file, it aborts with error code 3 (Disk full). For tsize in Read requests, the server tells the client how large the file is; if the client cannot handle it, the client aborts with the same error code.

The TFTP Option Extension mechanism ensures both ends agree on all options before data transfer begins, avoiding compatibility problems and allowing graceful fallback if options are not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending data, the client and server agree on timeout and size. If the receiver does not have room for the file, it says so before wasting time and bandwidth.
